game:astraterra-handbook-overview-text:
Astra Terra: Astronomy
The sky over this world is a real one. It turns with the hour, tilts with how far north or south you have walked, and shows you different figures in different seasons.

Over five thousand fixed stars stand above you, in the constellations of our own sky. Five planets wander among them. Meteor showers return each year, and four comets return on periods of their own, the longest of them once in about seventy-five world years.

None of it is labelled. The sky never tells you that a light is called Mars, or that a line of stars is called Orion — those are names people wrote in books. Astra Terra gives you the instruments and the empty book, and what gets written in it is yours.

Where to start
Craft a Brass Telescope, find a dark and cloudless night with open sky above you, and look up. Everything else follows from watching.

game:astraterra-handbook-nightsky-text:
Reading the night sky
The same stars, seen from a different place at a different hour, are a different sky.

Latitude. Walk north and the pole star climbs; walk south and it sinks, while stars you have never seen rise ahead of you. Near the poles some figures never set at all, and others can never rise. Every instrument here answers for the latitude you are standing at.

The turning of the night. The whole sky wheels through the night around the pole. A constellation low in the east after dusk is high overhead hours later. Its best moment is its transit, when it crosses the meridian at its highest.

The seasons. The stars also shift a little earlier each night, so the sky belongs to the season as much as to the hour. A figure that owns the winter evenings is lost in daylight in summer, and back again a year later.

Conditions for observing. To see and draw stars you need a sky dark enough, weather clear enough, and open air overhead — a roof or a hillside will stop you. The Calibrated Astrolabe is the exception: it predicts rather than observes, so it answers indoors, in daylight, and in bad weather.

Lying down. Press astraterra-liedown to lie on your back on the ground. In first person the view drops to the grass and turns straight up, so the sky fills the screen. Move, jump, or press it again to stand. Every instrument still works while you are lying down.

The Milky Way. On a properly dark night the stars stand against a broad band of glow: the light of far more stars than can be told apart, with a bright core towards the constellations of the south and dark dust lanes splitting it along its length. It turns with the rest of the sky. It is the faintest thing up there, so twilight takes it first and a bright moon washes most of it away — look for it near new moon, well after dusk.
game:astraterra-handbook-telescopes-text:
Telescopes
Glass, brass and a stick, and suddenly there are ten times as many stars.

The Brass Telescope is built from plain glass, brass and a stick. Hold rightmouse to raise it to your eye. While scoped:
• scroll to change zoom.
• middlemouse to cycle modes.

Observe looks. Centre a wandering star and press sneak to write it into your book and name it.
Draw makes constellations: drag with leftmouse from one guide star to another to lay down a segment.
Inspect names or renames a saved constellation you click on.
Remove Segment deletes the segment you click on.

Drawing and naming need a book in your off-hand and ink and quill in your inventory — see Constellations and the journal.

Deep sky objects — nebulae, galaxies, clusters — are invisible to the naked eye and only resolve under magnification. Zoom in on a faint smudge and see what it turns into.

The Precision Telescope is the same instrument built around the brass one, with ten far stronger zoom steps for careful work. It uses exactly the same modes.

A telescope is still a zoom tool when the sky is too bright or too cloudy for astronomy; only the star-specific work needs good conditions.
game:astraterra-handbook-sextant-text:
The Sextant
How high is it? Everything else in navigation starts with that question.

The Sextant is brass, plain glass, nails and strips, and a bit of silver for the scale. Hold rightmouse and put the centre of your view on the sun, the moon, a star, a planet or a comet. The readout at the top names what you sighted and gives its angle above the horizon in degrees. If several bodies fall in the sight, the one nearest the centre wins.

The sun and the moon can be shot whenever they are up, so the Sextant works in broad daylight. A daytime moon is a perfectly good sight, and usually an easier one than a star. Stars and planets need a dark enough sky.

While holding it, middlemouse cycles the display through the angle alone, the rose equatorial grid, the cyan azimuthal grid, and both together. Letting go restores whatever grid you set with .stars sky-grid; the Sextant remembers its own choice for the rest of the session.

Sneak while sighting to write the reading down. With a writable book in your left hand and ink and quill in your inventory, sneaking adds a dated entry: the angle, the bearing, the brightness, the day and hour, and the latitude you stood at. The entry never says what you sighted — only that something stood there, at that hour. Whether it was a fixed star or a wanderer is something you find out by sighting the same place again on another night. Angles are written to one arcminute, which is as fine as this Sextant reads.

A planet reads as Wandering star unless a book in your off-hand names it. Swap books and the sky is renamed at once.

If nothing readable is near the centre the readout tells you what there is to aim at instead, and if the sky above you is blocked it says so.

Sighting the sun costs you nothing here. A real navigator would use a shade glass.
game:astraterra-handbook-astrolabe-text:
The Calibrated Astrolabe
The telescope shows you what is there. The astrolabe tells you what will be.

Recover a ruined astrolabe from old buildings and combine it with a brass plate to fit it for use. Hold it in your main hand and a written constellation book in your off-hand, then hold rightmouse to open the planning readout.

Cutting the plate. An astrolabe is engraved for one latitude, and a new one is blank: it reads no plate and will not place a star. Stand under open sky after dusk and hold sneak + rightmouse for a few seconds while it sights the pole. A bar fills as it works, and tells you why if it will not — a roof overhead, or a sky still too bright. You need nothing but the sky for this.

Afterwards every answer it gives is for that latitude. Travel far enough and it starts reporting how far you have strayed; past about eight degrees it asks to be recut. Until then it is faithfully describing the sky over somewhere else.

Reading it. For the selected target it gives the compass direction, the angle above the horizon, whether it is rising or setting, how long until transit, and whether it is circumpolar or can never rise where you are.

Controls.
• middlemouse selects the next target: each constellation in the book, then the planets and comets.
• scroll forecasts an hour at a time.
• sneak + scroll forecasts seven days at a time.
• sneak + rightmouse recuts the plate for where you are now.

Forecasting spans a world year and follows this world's day and year length. A planet is forecast where it will actually be, not where it is now, and a comet that is away reads as the days until it returns. Let go and the forecast snaps back to the present.

The hour. The astrolabe also tells the time, read off the sun the way a nocturnal does: the hour of the day, whether it is daylight, dusk, night or dawn, the sun's angle above or below the horizon, and how long until the next sunrise or sunset. That clock is not engraved and never drifts, and it follows your forecast, so you can find the hour a constellation stands highest before committing to the wait. Near the poles, where the sun may not rise for a stretch of the year, it says so rather than inventing an hour. The time shows even with no book held.
game:astraterra-handbook-constellations-:
Constellations and the journal
A constellation is a line somebody decided to draw. This is the book you draw yours in.

Put a blank book in your off-hand and keep ink and quill in your inventory. Scope in with a telescope, switch to Draw, and drag from one guide star to another. The segment is written into the book.

Constellations are visible only while you hold the book they live in. That makes a written book a real object: hand it to another player and they see your figures, under your names.

Once Astra Terra writes the first constellation, ordinary book editing is locked, but the journal keeps working. Ink and quill are needed to create, add to, remove, rename, or build.

Commands
• .stars list — what is in the held book.
• .stars info selected — star and segment counts, the best visibility window, and the current state.
• .stars name, .stars select, .stars delete — manage entries.
• .stars build Ori — write one of the 88 authored figures straight into the book.

Built figures are ordinary journal entries afterwards: inspect, rename, or delete them like anything you drew by hand.
game:astraterra-handbook-wanderingstars-:
Wandering stars
Five of the lights up there are not stars, and no telescope will tell you which.

Through any eyepiece a planet stays a point of light exactly like the stars around it. What gives it away is that it moves. Chart a bright light over a few nights and if it has shifted against the fixed stars behind it, you have found one — which is how the ancients picked them out.

When you are satisfied, centre it in Observe mode and press sneak. It goes into your book and you are asked what to call it. Sneak rather than a click, because rightmouse is already busy holding the scope up. As with drawing, you need a book in your off-hand and ink and quill on you.

The name is yours. Nothing in the sky will ever tell you it was called Mars — that name only arrives in a book somebody else already wrote. Until then every instrument calls it a Wandering star.

The Calibrated Astrolabe lists all five planets whether or not they are up, marked as planets so they are not mistaken for a figure you drew. Being told that Saturn is below the horizon and transits in nine hours is exactly what the instrument is for.

Planets are usually among the brightest things in the sky, which makes them the easiest sights after the sun and the moon.
game:astraterra-handbook-cometsandshower:
Meteor showers and comets
The two things in the sky worth staying up for.

Meteor showers return at the same point of every world year, whatever length that year is. A shower is worth watching when its season is near the peak, its radiant is above the horizon, and the sky is dark. A bright moon drowns the faint meteors but not the brightest ones.

Every streak points back toward its shower's radiant. Streaks near that point are short and streaks far across the sky are long, because parallel paths seen in perspective look that way.

Comets return on their own periods, counted in world years: about every 5, 14, 33, and 75. Each is the parent of a shower already in the sky, so the dust you watch burn up some nights came off the comet you are waiting for.

An apparition lasts a couple of world weeks. The comet moves along its own track against the stars and brightens as it rounds perihelion before fading, and its tail and coma build and fade with it — for the first nights it is a faint smudge, and only near perihelion is it the finest thing in the sky.

The tail points away from the sun, not along the comet's motion, and swings right around as it passes perihelion. Sunlight and the solar wind push it, so it leans anti-sunward whichever way the comet is going.

The Sextant sights a comet like anything else, and a comet keeps its name without a book: where a planet is a discovery you make by watching, a comet is an event the sky announces. The Calibrated Astrolabe lists comets that are away as the days until they return, and forecasting that far ahead turns the line into a real position — so you can know where to be, and when, years before it arrives.
